The algorithm relies upon a built-in algebra of local Taylor-series expansions in order to compute highly accurate solutions to the set of differential equations characterizing first order conditions. It offers an extensive user friendly menu whereby one can assign commonly-used distributions to bidders and can also create arbitrary (non-inclusive) coalitions. In addition to (inverse) bid functions, the algorithm also computes a full range of auxiliary statistics of interest (expected rev- enues, probabilities of winning, probability of retention under reserve pricing and, on request, optimal reserve price). The algorithm also includes a built-in numerical pro- cedure designed to automatically produce local Taylor-series expansions for any user- supplied distribution, whether analytical or tabulated (empirical, parametric, semi- or non-parametric). It provides a tool of unparalleled flexibility for the numerical investi- gation of theoretical conjectures of interest and/or for easy implementation within any numerical empirical inference procedure relying upon inverse bid functions. We also provide operational univariate quadratures to evaluate probabilities of winning, as well as expected revenues for the bidders and the auctioneer. The latter is used to compute optimal reserves under asymmetric environments. This also enables us to provide insights as to whether collusion among subsets of bidders is sustainable. We first review some of the relevant literature. Much of the earlier auction literature as- sumed that bidders draw their signals from a common underlying distribution. Pioneering contributions include Riley and Samuelson (1981), Milgrom and Weber (1982), Matthews (1983), and Maskin and Riley (1984). Furthermore, under stochastic dominance, Maskin and Riley (2000a) show that the high-bid auction dominates the open-bid auction in terms of seller revenue and that the strong bidder (with the stochastically dominant distribution) shades his bid more than the weak bidder. They also provide examples of situations where the seller revenue is higher in open auctions than in high auctions. They proposed a numerical algorithm to compute first-price, equilibrium-bid functions in a two (subgroups of) players asymmetric environment under uniform distri- butions. In such games, private values are modelled as draws from bidder-specific type distributions and pay-your-bid rules are used to determine transactions prices. We provide a formal comparison of the performance of these numerical methods (based on speed and accuracy) and suggest ways in which they can be improved and extended as well as applied to new settings. Keywords: first-price auctions; asymmetric auctions; private-values model; numerical solutions. JEL Classification: C20, D44, L1. 1 Motivation and Introduction During the past half century, economists have made considerable progress in understanding the theoretical structure of strategic behavior under market mechanisms, such as auctions, when the number of potential participants is relatively small; see Krishna [2010] for a com- prehensive presentation and evaluation of progress. Perhaps the most significant breakthrough in understanding behavior at auctions was made by Vickrey [1961] who modelled auctions as noncooperative games of incomplete in- formation where bidders have private information concerning their type that they exploit when tendering offers for the good for sale. One analytic device commonly used to describe bidder motivation at auctions is a continuous random variable that represents individual- specific heterogeneity in types, which is typically interpreted as heterogeneity in valuations. The conceptual experiment involves each potential bidder receiving an independent draw from a distribution of valuations. Conditional on his draw, a bidder is assumed to act purposefully, maximizing either the expected profit or the expected utility of profit from winning the good for sale. Another frequently-made assumption is that the bidders are ex ante symmetric, their independent draws coming from the same distribution of valuations, an assumption that then allows the researcher to focus on a representative agent's decision rule 2 when characterizing the Bayes-Nash equilibrium to the auction game, particularly under the pay-your-bid pricing rule, often referred to as first-price auctions, at least by economists.1 The assumption of symmetry is made largely for computational convenience. When the draws of potential bidders are independent, but from different distributions--urns, if you like--then the system of first-order differential equations that characterizes a Bayes-Nash equilibrium usually does not have a convenient closed-form solution: typically, approximate solutions can only be calculated numerically.2 Asymmetries may exist in practice for any number of reasons in addition to the standard heterogeneous-distributions case. For example, an asymmetric first-price model is relevant when bidders are assumed to draw valuations from the same distribution, but have different preferences (for instance, risk-averse bidders might differ by their Arrow-Pratt coefficient of relative risk aversion), when bidders collude and form coalitions, and when the auction- eer (perhaps the government) grants preference to a class of bidders. Bid preferences are particularly interesting because the auctioneer, for whatever reason, deliberately introduces an asymmetry when evaluating bids, even though bidders may be symmetric. In addition, admitting several objects complicates matters considerably; see, for example, Weber [1983]. In fact, economic theorists distinguish between multi-object and multi-unit auctions. At multi-unit auctions, it matters not which unit a bidder wins, but rather the aggregate num- ber of units he wins, while at multi-object auctions it matters which specific object(s) a bidder wins. An example of a multi-object auction would involve the sale of an apple and an orange, while an example of a multi-unit auction would involve the sale of two identical apples. fetched_contents.text: Asymmetric auctions: Perturbations, ε- equilibrium, and equilibrium 1. Introduction We use a perturbation approach to show the existence of and characterize the Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE) in first-price auctions with independent and private valuations (which we refer to hereafter as auctions) with asymmetric supports. We then show that BNE in auctions with asymmetric supports are continuous and piece-wise differentiable over the valuations where a player can win with a positive probability. Consequently, ε-BNE converges uniformly to BNE, and the approximation of BNE by ε-BNE is precise. Our perturbation approach handles the existence, characterization, and computation of BNE and ε-BNE in one shot. Literature on first-price auctions1 usually characterizes the BNE through a system of ordinary differential equations. Structure of the equilibrium bidding strategy

In asymmetric first-price auctions, the equilibrium bidding strategy is typically not symmetric, and the form of the bid function depends on the bidder’s private value distribution and the distribution of the opponent. The evidence indicates that numerical methods are often used to compute these strategies, especially when bidders draw independent private values from heterogeneous distributions [N2-R1][N2-F1]. One numerical paper explicitly states that it proposes a powerful, fully automated, and numerically robust algorithm to compute (inverse) equilibrium bid functions for asymmetric, independent private values, first-price auctions [N2-F1]. That paper also emphasizes that it can handle arbitrary distributions, whether analytical or tabulated, and provides inverse bid functions along with other auxiliary statistics such as probabilities of winning and expected revenues [N2-F1].

The practical example provided by the Mathematics Stack Exchange question illustrates the core structure: for a two-bidder asymmetric auction, the bidder’s optimal bid depends on solving a system of differential equations derived from the first-order conditions of the optimization problem [N5-F4]. In that example, the bidder’s valuation is mapped through an inverse-bid function, and the first-order condition is translated into a differential equation involving the opponent’s inverse-bid function [N5-F4]. This shows that the equilibrium strategy is determined by a coupled system of equations rather than a single one-sided formula. The example also notes that the resulting equations can be hand-wavy to solve formally, which reflects the general difficulty of deriving explicit analytical solutions in asymmetric cases [N5-F4].

The form of the equilibrium bid function is therefore determined by the private value distribution and the opponent’s distribution. The numerical paper states that the algorithm can assign commonly-used distributions to bidders and also create arbitrary (non-inclusive) coalitions, implying that the strategy depends directly on the specific distributional parameters of each bidder [N2-F1]. In the example, bidder 1’s distribution is F1(x) = 1/4(x − 1)² over [1, 3], and bidder 2’s is exp(2/3x − 2) over [0, 3], which are both specific, non-standard distributions [N5-F4]. The equilibrium strategies derived are β1(x) = x − 1 and β2(x) = 2/3x, showing that the strategy is tied to the distributional support and the functional form of each bidder’s value distribution [N5-F4].

As for the role of reserve prices or other auction rules, the evidence is mixed but clear in one direction: reserve prices are explicitly part of the numerical solution environment. The numerical paper says it also computes probability of retention under reserve pricing and can be used to compute optimal reserve price under asymmetric environments [N2-F1]. That means reserve prices can affect the equilibrium strategy by changing the set of feasible bids and the winning probabilities, and the numerical algorithm accounts for that in its solution. However, the provided evidence does not establish a general closed-form reserve-price effect on the bid function; it only shows that reserve pricing is a relevant auxiliary feature of the solution framework [N2-F1].

Whether the strategies are symmetric, asymmetric, or mixed is directly answered by the evidence: in asymmetric first-price auctions, the strategies are generally asymmetric because the bidders have different distributions [N2-R1][N2-F1]. The example also supports this by showing two different bidding functions for two different bidders [N5-F4]. The evidence does not support a general symmetric equilibrium in the asymmetric case, and the existence literature cited below suggests that asymmetric equilibria are the norm, not the exception, when distributions differ [N4-F3][N4-R4]. Therefore, the equilibrium strategy is asymmetric in general, not symmetric.

Overall, the equilibrium bidding strategy in asymmetric first-price auctions is typically asymmetric, determined by the bidder’s private value distribution and the opponent’s distribution, and often computed numerically because analytical solutions are difficult or nonexistent for heterogeneous distributions [N2-F1][N5-F4]. The strategy can also be influenced by reserve prices and other auction rules, but the provided evidence emphasizes the numerical solution approach rather than an explicit closed-form analytical solution [N2-F1][N2-R1].

Special cases and simplifying assumptions that make the problem tractable

When bidders have identical distributions, the problem becomes simpler and more tractable, but it is still not symmetric in the same way as the standard symmetric auction literature. The evidence indicates that existence and uniqueness results under asymmetry can be found in Lebrun (1996, 1999, 2006) or Maskin and Riley (2000a, 2000b) [N4-F3]. However, the numerical paper explicitly notes that much earlier auction literature assumed common distributions and that results such as revenue equivalence obtain under symmetry [N2-F1]. That implies that identical distributions are a special case where analytical results are often available, but they are not the general asymmetric case.

When one bidder has a discrete or simple distribution, the problem becomes more tractable numerically because the numerical algorithms can handle arbitrary distributions, including tabulated or empirical ones [N2-F1]. The example provided by the Mathematics Stack Exchange question uses a specific continuous distribution for each bidder, but the numerical paper explicitly states that it can handle arbitrary distributions and that its built-in procedure can produce local Taylor-series expansions for any user-supplied distribution [N2-F1]. That means even discrete or simple distributions can be handled, although the evidence here does not give a concrete example of a discrete case. Still, the general point is clear: numerical methods can accommodate simpler distributions as special cases [N2-F1].

When there are reserve prices or bidder dominance, the problem can still be tractable, but the numerical solution must account for these features explicitly. The numerical paper says it also computes probability of retention under reserve pricing and can compute optimal reserve price under asymmetric environments [N2-F1]. That means reserve pricing is not automatically trivial; instead, it affects the equilibrium strategy and must be included in the solution. The evidence does not provide a general formula for how dominance translates into strategy, but it does show that the solution framework can incorporate reserve prices and asymmetric dominance through its numerical algorithm [N2-F1]. In other words, bidder dominance is a parameter that can be handled numerically rather than being ignored.

How bidder asymmetry can be parameterized in practice is also supported by the numerical paper’s description of the algorithm: it allows users to assign commonly-used distributions to bidders and can create arbitrary (non-inclusive) coalitions [N2-F1]. This implies that asymmetry can be parameterized by assigning different distributions to different bidders, and the algorithm can handle that without requiring the distributions to be identical or even close in form. The example also illustrates this by specifying different functional forms for each bidder’s value distribution [N5-F4]. In practice, asymmetry can therefore be parameterized by specifying each bidder’s distribution separately, and the numerical solution method can then compute the equilibrium accordingly [N2-F1][N5-F4].

In summary, the special cases that make the problem tractable are: identical distributions, which allow more analytical results and are common in auction theory [N2-F1]; discrete or simple distributions, which numerical methods can still handle [N2-F1]; reserve prices, which can be incorporated into the equilibrium computation [N2-F1]; and bidder dominance, which can be modeled through asymmetric distributional parameters [N2-F1]. The overall takeaway is that asymmetry is the default for the problem, but it becomes tractable when distributions are simple, when reserve prices are included, and when numerical algorithms are used [N2-F1][N5-F4].

The evidence also mentions the boundary-value method, a novel method for computing equilibrium bids in asymmetric first-price auctions [N3-R4]. The evidence further notes that numerical methods can be compared in terms of speed and accuracy, and that they can be improved and extended for new settings [N3-F2]. This suggests that the solution method choice is practical and depends on the problem’s complexity, speed requirements, and desired accuracy.

Practical limitations and approximations are significant. The perturbation paper says the characterization of BNE rests on an ill-posed DAE, making a direct numerical solution “out of hand,” and that the perturbation approach is needed to make the problem tractable [N4-F3]. It also states that the ε-BNE characterization is well-posed, which allows for precise approximation and computation [N4-F3]. The evidence also notes that numerical methods can be used with arbitrary distributions, including empirical or non-parametric ones, but that the lower end-point of the differential equations is often poorly behaved, requiring careful numerical handling [N4-F3]. In other words, practical limitations include ill-conditioning, boundary behavior, and the need for robust numerical algorithms.

Boundary-value or backward-indifference methods work by transforming the equilibrium problem into a well-posed numerical problem.
